moduleTitle: Pilgrimage: the study of one place of Roman Catholic pilgrimage and different Christian views

note.specFocus: AQA 8062 Catholic Christianity, worship: the role and importance of pilgrimage, including the study of one place of Roman Catholic pilgrimage (Lourdes is used here; Walsingham, Rome and the Holy Land are noted), and different Christian views about the importance of pilgrimage.
note.summary:
KEY IDEA: A pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place for a religious purpose. Catholics believe "pilgrimages evoke our earthly journey toward heaven and are traditionally very special occasions for renewal in prayer" (CCC 2691). The Church itself is described as a "pilgrim people" on its way to God (Lumen Gentium 48; Hebrews 13:14, "here we have no lasting city"). Pilgrimage is a form of popular piety (CCC 1674).

PURPOSES: to grow closer to God and deepen faith; to pray in a place where God's presence is felt to be strong ("thin places"); to seek healing of body or spirit; to ask for forgiveness or do penance; to give thanks; to honour Mary or a saint; to experience community with other believers; and to take time out from daily life to reflect. The journey matters as well as the destination, because it can involve sacrifice and simplicity. Jesus himself went on pilgrimage to Jerusalem for Passover (Luke 2:41–42), and the Psalms include "Songs of Ascents" sung by pilgrims ("I was glad when they said to me, 'Let us go to the house of the LORD!'", Psalm 122:1).

STUDY OF ONE PLACE: LOURDES (France). AQA lets you choose any Catholic pilgrimage site, and Lourdes is the most commonly studied.
• History: in 1858, at the Grotto of Massabielle, 14-year-old Bernadette Soubirous reported 18 apparitions of a "Lady" (from 11 February). The Lady asked for prayer and penance and for a chapel to be built, and told Bernadette to dig at a spot where a spring began to flow. On 25 March the Lady said, "I am the Immaculate Conception", confirming a doctrine Pope Pius IX had defined in 1854. The Church recognised the apparitions in 1862. Bernadette became a nun and was canonised in 1933.
• What pilgrims do: pray at the Grotto, drink or bathe in the spring water (the baths), attend Mass (including in the vast underground basilica), join the nightly torchlight Marian procession singing the "Lourdes Ave Maria", and take part in the Eucharistic procession and blessing of the sick. Many go to the Sacrament of Reconciliation, light candles and buy holy water.
• Healing: the Lourdes Medical Bureau investigates claimed cures. Thousands of cures have been reported, but the Church has officially recognised only about 70 as miracles. For most pilgrims the "healing" is spiritual: peace, acceptance and renewed faith.
• Today: millions of people visit each year. Many dioceses in Britain run annual pilgrimages with sick and disabled pilgrims, supported by young volunteers (helpers) and organisations such as HCPT, which takes disabled and disadvantaged children. The volunteering and care for the sick are themselves an expression of faith.

OTHER CATHOLIC SITES: Rome (tombs of St Peter and St Paul; Jubilee Years, such as the 2025 "Pilgrims of Hope" Jubilee with Holy Doors); the Holy Land (Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Via Dolorosa); Walsingham, "England's Nazareth" (1061, Lady Richeldis), with both Catholic and Anglican shrines; Fatima (Portugal, 1917); Knock (Ireland, 1879); Santiago de Compostela (Camino).

DIFFERENT CHRISTIAN VIEWS:
• Catholics and Orthodox: pilgrimage is a valuable act of devotion, encouraged but not compulsory.
• Anglicans: many go to Walsingham, Iona or the Holy Land.
• Many Protestants, following the Reformers, are suspicious of pilgrimage. They argue that God is equally present everywhere ("true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth", John 4:21–24) and that pilgrimage can encourage superstition or the idea of earning grace. Some Protestants visit the Holy Land as educational trips rather than pilgrimages.
• Quakers do not practise pilgrimage, and some Christians see life itself as the true pilgrimage, or think the money is better given to the poor.

KEY TERMS: pilgrimage, shrine, apparition, Immaculate Conception, grotto, Marian procession, miracle, Jubilee, penance.

questions.question:
Who reported seeing apparitions of Mary at Lourdes in 1858?
A) St Teresa of Calcutta
B) Bernadette Soubirous
C) Lady Richeldis de Faverches
D) St Francis of Assisi
questions.modelAnswer:
Answer: B) Bernadette Soubirous.

She reported 18 apparitions at the Grotto of Massabielle in 1858. Richeldis is linked to Walsingham (1061). Mother Teresa and Francis of Assisi are unconnected to Lourdes.
questions.examTip: Know the key facts of your chosen pilgrimage site: who, when, what happened and what pilgrims do.

questions.question:
Which place of Catholic pilgrimage in England is known as 'England's Nazareth'?
A) Canterbury
B) Lindisfarne
C) Walsingham
D) Iona
questions.modelAnswer:
Answer: C) Walsingham (Norfolk).

According to tradition, in 1061 Lady Richeldis had a vision and built a replica of the Holy House of Nazareth there. Iona is in Scotland and is associated with an ecumenical community. Canterbury and Lindisfarne are linked to St Thomas Becket and St Cuthbert.
questions.examTip: Iona is Scotland, not England. Watch for geographical distractors.

questions.question: Give one reason why a Catholic might go on pilgrimage.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one from: to grow closer to God; to pray in a holy place; to seek healing; to ask forgiveness / do penance; to give thanks; to honour Mary or a saint; to strengthen faith; to meet other believers; to reflect away from daily life; to help the sick (as a volunteer).
questions.examTip: Only your first reason is marked. Pick the clearest one.

questions.question: Give one activity that pilgrims take part in at Lourdes.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one from: praying at the Grotto; bathing in or drinking the spring water; attending Mass; the torchlight (Marian) procession; the Eucharistic procession / blessing of the sick; going to Confession; lighting candles; volunteering to help sick pilgrims.
questions.examTip: Make it specific to the site. 'Torchlight procession' is better than 'praying'.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which going on pilgrimage might influence a Catholic.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: A pilgrimage can strengthen a Catholic's faith (1 mark). Praying at a holy place like the Grotto at Lourdes, alongside thousands of others in the torchlight procession, can make them feel closer to God and part of the worldwide Church. Many return home with a renewed commitment to prayer and Mass (2nd mark).

Second way: Pilgrimage can lead a Catholic to serve others (1 mark). Many young people go to Lourdes as volunteers with diocesan pilgrimages or HCPT, caring for sick and disabled pilgrims. This experience can inspire them to keep helping vulnerable people at home, for example by joining the SVP (2nd mark).
questions.examTip: Influence questions can be about inner change (faith) as well as outer actions (service). Use one of each.

questions.question: Explain two different Christian views about pilgrimage.
questions.modelAnswer:
First view: Catholics believe pilgrimage is a valuable act of worship and devotion (1 mark). Holy places like Lourdes, Rome and Jerusalem help believers pray, seek healing and grow in faith. The Catechism says pilgrimages 'evoke our earthly journey toward heaven' (CCC 2691) (2nd mark).

Second view: Many Protestant Christians believe pilgrimage is unnecessary (1 mark). They argue that God is present everywhere and can be worshipped 'in spirit and truth' anywhere (John 4:23). Some worry pilgrimage can encourage superstition about holy water or relics, or the idea of earning God's favour, and that the money could be better spent on the poor (2nd mark).
questions.examTip: Give the reason for each view. A Bible verse makes the Protestant view much stronger.

questions.question:
Explain two reasons why Lourdes is an important place of pilgrimage for Catholics.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First reason: Catholics believe Mary appeared there to Bernadette Soubirous in 1858 (1 mark). The Lady called herself 'the Immaculate Conception' and asked for prayer and penance. The Church recognised the apparitions in 1862, so pilgrims go to honour Mary and respond to her call to conversion (2nd mark).

Second reason: Lourdes is associated with healing (1 mark). Pilgrims, especially the sick, bathe in or drink the spring water that began to flow when Bernadette dug at the Lady's request. About 70 cures have been officially recognised as miracles, and many more people report spiritual healing such as peace and strength to cope with illness (2nd mark).

Source of authority: The Catechism teaches that 'pilgrimages evoke our earthly journey toward heaven and are traditionally very special occasions for renewal in prayer' (CCC 2691). Lourdes is important because it offers this renewal. At the Grotto, in the processions and at Mass, pilgrims renew their prayer and remember that life is a journey towards God (2 marks).
questions.examTip: If you study a different site (e.g. Walsingham, Rome), the same structure works: history, plus what it offers pilgrims, plus a source.

questions.question:
Explain two purposes of Catholic pilgrimage.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First purpose: To grow closer to God through prayer (1 mark). Away from the distractions of everyday life, pilgrims spend time at Mass, in prayer and in quiet reflection at a holy place, which can deepen their relationship with God (2nd mark).

Second purpose: To seek forgiveness and spiritual healing (1 mark). A pilgrimage can be an act of penance. The effort of the journey and the chance to receive the sacrament of Reconciliation help people to turn away from sin and make a fresh start. Some also seek physical healing (2nd mark).

Source of authority: Psalm 122 begins, 'I was glad when they said to me, "Let us go to the house of the LORD!"' It was a song of Jewish pilgrims travelling to Jerusalem, and Jesus himself went to Jerusalem for Passover (Luke 2:41). This shows that journeying to a holy place to worship God is rooted in scripture and in the example of Jesus (2 marks).
questions.examTip: 'Purpose' means why, so start each point with 'to…'.

questions.question:
'Pilgrimage is a waste of time and money.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• refer to Catholic teaching
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Christians believe God is everywhere. Jesus told the Samaritan woman that true worshippers would worship 'in spirit and truth', not only on a particular mountain or in Jerusalem (John 4:21–24). If God can be met in a local church, at home or in nature, travelling hundreds of miles to a shrine seems unnecessary. Many Protestant Christians, following the Reformers, hold this view.

Pilgrimage can be expensive. A trip to Lourdes, Rome or the Holy Land can cost hundreds or thousands of pounds, which could instead be given to the poor. Jesus taught that serving 'the least of these' is serving him (Matthew 25:40). Some sites have become commercialised, with souvenir shops and crowds, and critics argue that some practices, such as collecting holy water, can become superstitious. A humanist may also see claims of miraculous healing as unproven.

ARGUMENTS AGAINST

The Catholic Church teaches that pilgrimages 'evoke our earthly journey toward heaven and are traditionally very special occasions for renewal in prayer' (CCC 2691). Being somewhere holy, where saints have prayed or where Mary is believed to have appeared, can help people feel God's presence powerfully and change their lives. Many pilgrims return with deeper faith, peace or healing of fear and grief.

Pilgrimage has deep roots in scripture. Jewish pilgrims sang Psalm 122, 'Let us go to the house of the LORD', and Jesus travelled to Jerusalem for Passover (Luke 2:41). The Church calls itself a 'pilgrim people', so pilgrimage is a living image of the Christian life.

Pilgrimage often includes service. At Lourdes, thousands of volunteers, many of them young people, care for sick and disabled pilgrims, and groups like HCPT give children holidays they would never otherwise have. The experience of community, sacrifice and care for others can last a lifetime. It is not wasted. Many pilgrimages are also affordable or local, such as walking to Walsingham or a diocesan shrine.

CONCLUSION

The statement is right that God is present everywhere and that money spent on travel could help the poor. A pilgrimage made only for tourism or superstition would be hard to justify. However, for Catholics, a pilgrimage can bring real spiritual renewal, express faith publicly and involve practical love for the sick. It also has a basis in scripture and Church teaching. The more convincing view is that pilgrimage is not a waste when it is made with the right intentions, though it is not essential, and Catholics should balance it with their duty to the poor.
questions.examTip: Use concrete examples from your chosen site (Lourdes processions, volunteers, cures). They turn general points into strong evidence.

questions.question:
'Pilgrimage is the best way for a Catholic to grow closer to God.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• refer to Catholic teaching
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

A pilgrimage takes a person out of ordinary routines and devotes days or weeks to God. At a site such as Lourdes, pilgrims attend Mass daily, go to Confession, pray at the Grotto and join thousands of others in processions. This concentrated experience can be more intense than anything at home. Many people describe a pilgrimage as a turning point in their faith.

Holy places can make faith feel real. Walking where Jesus walked in Jerusalem, or praying at St Peter's tomb in Rome, links pilgrims with the history of their faith. The Catechism describes pilgrimages as 'very special occasions for renewal in prayer' (CCC 2691). The sacrifice involved, such as walking the Camino to Santiago, can deepen humility and trust in God.

ARGUMENTS AGAINST

The Catholic Church teaches that the Eucharist, not pilgrimage, is 'the source and summit of the Christian life' (Lumen Gentium 11). Catholics can receive Christ himself at any Sunday Mass in their local parish. Pilgrimage is a form of popular piety, which the Church says supports the liturgy but 'does not replace it' (CCC 1675). On this view, the best way to grow closer to God is regular Mass, prayer and the sacraments.

Daily prayer is available to everyone, every day, whereas most people go on pilgrimage rarely or never. Jesus taught his followers to pray to the Father 'in secret' (Matthew 6:6), and St Paul says 'pray without ceasing' (1 Thessalonians 5:17). Growing closer to God is a lifelong process, not a one-off trip.

Loving one's neighbour is also a way to meet God. Jesus says 'just as you did it to one of the least of these… you did it to me' (Matthew 25:40). Volunteering with the SVP or a food bank may bring a person closer to Christ than travelling to a shrine. Many Protestants would add that God is equally present everywhere (John 4:23), so special places are not needed. Some people with disabilities or little money cannot travel at all, so pilgrimage cannot be the 'best' way for everyone.

CONCLUSION

Pilgrimage can be a powerful, life-changing way to grow closer to God, especially as a time of renewal. But Catholic teaching places the Eucharist and the sacraments at the centre of the spiritual life, together with daily prayer and love of neighbour. These are available to all, all the time. The more convincing conclusion is that pilgrimage is a valuable extra that can refresh faith, but it is not the best way. Regular Mass and prayer, lived out in service, matter more.
questions.examTip: Compare pilgrimage with everyday practices (Mass, prayer, service). Weighing alternatives is what earns Level 4.
